summary: This best current practice document discusses how to select secondary DNS servers for a zone, how many servers are appropriate, and some general maintenance issues for secondaries.

plainLanguage.summary: Advice on choosing backup phone books and how many to keep.

subtitle: How many backup DNS servers a zone needs, where to put them, and how to fix a broken zone serial number.

tldr.problem: Many DNS problems come from poor choices of secondary servers: all servers in one place, unreachable servers listed, or too few or too many servers.
tldr.mechanism: Place secondaries at topologically and geographically dispersed locations, list only servers resolvers can reach, use about three listed servers for most zones, and change zone serial numbers only by increments.
tldr.outcome: The guidance gives zone operators concrete rules for server placement, server counts and serial number repair.

today: RFC 2182 is a Best Current Practice published in July 1997, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Secondary Servers Matter
sections.content:
A zone is a part of the DNS tree treated as a unit. The DNS requires multiple servers for every delegated zone. One is usually the primary server, which holds the master copy of the zone file, and the others are secondary servers that obtain the zone from it by a zone transfer.

The RFC opens by saying that a number of DNS operational problems are attributable to poor choices of secondary servers. Placement and the diversity of network connectivity can raise a zone's reliability and improve network performance, while other choices can unexpectedly lower reliability.

To the rest of the DNS, the primary and secondary distinction does not matter. All servers are treated equally, even by the parent that delegates the zone.
sections.plainLanguage: One server keeps the master copy of a zone's records, and others keep copies. Anyone asking can use any of them.

sections.title: Choosing Where to Put Servers
sections.content:
Servers should be placed so that at least one is likely available to all significant parts of the Internet for any likely failure. Putting all servers at the local site is easy to manage but a poor policy, since one failed link or a site, building or room power failure could disconnect them all.

Secondary servers must be placed at both topologically and geographically dispersed locations, and connected through quite diverse paths. Placing all servers on the same LAN segment in the same room of the same building almost defeats the purpose of having multiple servers.

The RFC also rejects a myth, that name servers need not be reachable if the hosts in the domain are unreachable. Its reasons: clients react differently to failing to resolve than to failing to connect; a missing result is not cached, so failure to resolve adds network load; and not all names in a zone resolve to addresses inside the detached network.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not keep all your spare keys in the same drawer. Spread them across different places so one accident cannot lock you out.

sections.title: Unreachable Servers
sections.content:
Listing servers that large parts of the network cannot reach, such as a machine behind a firewall or a secondary address on a dual-homed host, adds no reliability and can lower it. Resolvers can only discover an address is unreachable by trying it and waiting for a timeout, which looks the same as packet loss, so they must retry several times. The probing may take so long that the client decides there is no answer, and it all adds traffic and load across the network.

Servers on intermittent connections should be treated as if behind a firewall. A Network Address Translator (NAT) is a similar problem, because in practice NATs translate only header addresses, not addresses embedded in DNS packets. An Application Layer Gateway (ALG) can help, but the solution below is likely still better.

The remedy is that NS records returned in any response should list only servers the requesting resolver is likely able to reach, and any resolver it may forward to. Since a server's addresses form a Resource Record Set, all must be returned or none: it is not acceptable to drop unreachable addresses or give them a low TTL. This usually needs dual DNS setups, one internal and one external. A server at a firewall boundary should be given two names, one per side, and treated as two servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Only give out phone numbers that actually ring for the person calling. Handing out dead numbers makes callers waste time trying them.

sections.title: How Many Servers and Which Ones
sections.content:
The DNS specification and domain registration rules require at least two servers for every zone. Two carefully placed servers are often enough, but not always: if one is down for a long time, the zone runs on just one, and may at times have none working. The RFC therefore advises more than two listed servers.

Many servers add little benefit and some cost. Responses get larger, and there is a limit to the size of a DNS packet, so it is wise to stay well clear of it. More servers also raise the chance that one is misconfigured without being noticed. The RFC recommends three servers for most organization-level zones, with at least one well removed from the others. Four or even five may suit zones needing higher reliability, with two or occasionally three of five at the local site.

Reverse zones, under .IN-ADDR.ARPA, are typically less crucial and often need fewer, less distributed servers. Stealth servers are authoritative for a zone but not listed in NS records, and are not counted. Having local servers be stealth servers lets a site answer local queries even if external communications fail, without making the rest of the Internet try to contact every server at the site.

Finding secondaries is usually easy: the suggested approach is to swap secondary service with an organization of similar size, which loses no confidential data because the zone data is public anyway.
sections.plainLanguage: Two spare copies can both be missing on a bad day, so keep three. Keeping a hundred just makes more things to look after.

sections.title: Fixing a Zone Serial Number
sections.content:
Secondaries use the serial number in the zone's SOA record to know when to update their copy. It is a 32 bit unsigned integer that wraps around, and it must be incremented every time the primary's zone changes. A serial number cannot be decremented.

If an editing error sets it too high, never simply decrease it. Secondaries will ignore the change, and ignore later increments until the earlier large value is exceeded. Instead, increment it several times, by less than 2^31 (2147483648) each step, waiting each time until all secondaries have updated.

The worked example: a serial that should be 10 was accidentally set to 1000, and the goal is 11. Set it to 2000000000, then 4000000000, then 11. Serial numbers wrap at 2^32 (4294967296), so 11 is an increment from 4000000000. It is essential to verify every server at each step. The RFC notes that it is possible in two steps with more aggressive values, but that takes more care.

Some nameservers do not implement serial arithmetic correctly. The RFC calls these defective, and says the usual cure is to ask the administrator to purge the zone and reload it from the primary. A defective server can be detected by waiting for at least the SOA refresh time and querying for the SOA to see if it still has the old serial.
sections.plainLanguage: Version numbers on a document can only go up. If you wrote a too-big number by mistake, you cannot go back; you have to count up past the top until you wrap around to the right place.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it is not believed to add to or lessen any security issues of the DNS. It does warn that compromise of a server for a domain can, in some situations, compromise the security of hosts in the domain, so care should be taken in choosing secondary servers to minimise this threat.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone takes over one of the servers that tells people where things are, they might send visitors to the wrong places, so pick trustworthy helpers.
